html:
The Tet Offensive began on the night of 30 January 1968, at Tet, the Vietnamese new year. About 80,000 North Vietnamese and Viet Cong fighters attacked more than 100 towns and cities across South Vietnam. They were beaten back, but the attack turned American opinion against the Vietnam War.

The leaders in Hanoi hoped a surprise attack on the cities would break the South Vietnamese army and start an uprising. Neither happened. In Saigon a squad got into the grounds of the American embassy and was killed within hours. The fight for Huế lasted a month and ruined much of the old imperial city; the communists killed about 3,000 civilians there. Tens of thousands of attackers died, and the Viet Cong never recovered its strength. Smaller waves followed in May and August.

Americans had been told the war was nearly won. Now they watched fighting in the streets of Saigon on television. When the army asked for 206,000 more men, President Lyndon Johnson said no. On 31 March he cut back the bombing of the North and said he would not run again. The United States began to pull its troops out in 1969. See the Fall of Saigon.
